source.title: Optimizing Information-theoretical Generalization Bounds via Anisotropic Noise in SGLD
source.authors: Bo-Han Wang; Hui-Shuai Zhang; Jieyu Zhang; Qi Meng; Wei Chen; Tie-Yan Liu

record.file_problem: none; full paper and supplementary materials are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study experimentally compares training and generalization errors under different SGLD noise covariances, using a different intervention from the listed versions.
record.gate_note: The study reports SGLD noise-structure comparisons and gradient-covariance measurements. It does not test the listed versions' random-label memorization, width, architecture, adaptive-optimizer, batch-size, dropout, sharpness, or memorized-example claims. Results cited from prior work are not extracted as rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests how SGLD noise covariance affects training loss and generalization gaps. None of its experiments or theoretical arguments tests V1–V8. Covariance anisotropy is not magnitude-aware weight sharpness, and comparing SGLD noise structures is not an adaptive-optimizer or batch-size comparison.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. More precisely, the authors derive covariance-trace constraints and a new information-theoretical bound, then optimize that bound using greedy or fixed priors. With the greedy prior, the optimum is proportional to the square root of population gradient covariance. Experiments using its empirical counterpart show smaller generalization gaps than isotropic noise at similar training loss. This establishes neither globally optimal test performance nor the bound's tightness.
record.recipe_differences: The study optimizes or compares SGLD noise covariances; it does not reproduce the methods in the listed claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise covariance structure and covariance-trace scale affect the reported generalization-error comparisons. The covariance trace constraint is associated with nearly coincident training-error curves for empirical-covariance and matched isotropic noise.

fits_no_version.finding: SREC-SGLD has a smaller generalization gap than isotropic SGLD at both tested covariance-trace scales, with nearly matching training-loss curves; it also has the smallest gap in the three-method comparison.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For this Fashion-MNIST convolutional network, square-root empirical-gradient-covariance noise reduces the generalization gap relative to isotropic noise at matched covariance trace.

fits_no_version.finding: EC-SGLD and isotropic SGLD have nearly coincident training curves when covariance traces match; matching Hessian-weighted traces leaves a substantial convergence difference.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Covariance trace is a useful empirical constraint for comparing training convergence across the tested SGLD noise structures.

fits_no_version.finding: SREC-SGLD more closely follows SGD's generalization-gap behavior than isotropic SGLD does.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Square-root empirical-gradient-covariance noise better approximates SGD's generalization-gap trajectory in this experiment.

fits_no_version.finding: The empirical gradient covariance is highly anisotropic along both SGD and Iso-SGLD training trajectories.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gradient-covariance energy concentrates in a small parameter subspace in the tested Fashion-MNIST network.

record.problems: The experimental evidence is limited to Fashion-MNIST and one four-layer convolutional network. Main comparisons are presented in figures without numeric error values or uncertainty estimates. The analytic optimization concerns information-theoretical bounds; the experiment reports generalization errors but does not establish the theoretical bound's tightness.
record.rows_left_out: None. All extractable experimental comparisons and gradient-covariance measurements relevant to the claim's subject are included; figure-only numerical values were not reconstructed.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label versus random-label held-out accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width needed for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning and recovery recipes.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adaptations that remove the penalty.
Dropout effects, small-data regimes, underfitting, and removal with weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because none measures a listed version; this does not negate the explicitly reported findings. References to original sources and prior large-batch results provide background rather than independent tests.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance on natural labels.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning or decay recipes.
Large-batch comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and adapted recipes.
Magnitude-aware sharpness measurements and their relation to generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples and measuring the resulting test-accuracy change.

rows.subject: empirical gradient covariance for SGD
rows.size_stated: 11330-dimensional parameter space; top 100 eigenvalues used to approximate the covariance
rows.operation_detail: Measured the ratio of the largest to the 500th-largest eigenvalue of the empirical gradient covariance.
rows.baseline: isotropic Gaussian eigenvalue ratio around 1.1 for dimension 11330
rows.note: The text reports the approximate ratios and states that the covariance energy concentrates in a small subspace.
rows.check: Gradient-covariance anisotropy does not measure V7's weight-perturbation sharpness. The top-100 approximation describes covariance construction, not how a 500th eigenvalue is measured. The extracted value 107 may flatten superscript notation and should not be treated as an unambiguous numerical value.
